title: The first bat mitzvah (1922)
hook: Judith Kaplan becomes a bat mitzvah in New York

segments.voice: Yesterday, Regina Jonas, and two heavy words: the first. Did you say a pioneer's name out loud? Today, a different kind of first, much smaller, on a Shabbat morning in New York. Day one thousand forty.

A Shabbat morning in a synagogue in New York, in 1922. The Torah has been read, the way it is every week. Then a girl named Judith Kaplan walks up to the front. Her father is the rabbi, Mordecai Kaplan, and he has decided that what boys do at this age, his daughter will do too. She says the blessings. She reads a passage of Torah aloud, in Hebrew and then in English, from a printed book. Then she sits down. That's all. There was no party plan, no theme, no DJ. And with it, the bat mitzvah as many Jews now know it began to take shape.
screen: `A SHABBAT MORNING IN NEW YORK.` → `A GIRL WALKS TO THE FRONT.` → `SHE SAYS THE BLESSINGS.`

segments.voice: Start with the words. Bar mitzvah, for a boy, and bat mitzvah, for a girl, mean son and daughter of the commandment. In Jewish law, a child grows into the age of the commandments: from then on, the mitzvot are theirs to keep, not just their parents' to teach. That happens to a girl whether there is a ceremony or not. What Judith Kaplan's Shabbat added was a public moment to mark it, in front of the community. Notice how careful the first one was. She did not read from the scroll itself. She read from a printed book, after the regular reading, standing a little apart. Even so, people noticed. Her father was a rabbi who wanted Judaism to change with the lives Jews actually lived, and he later founded the movement called Reconstructionist Judaism. For him, a girl standing up in the synagogue was part of that. Then the idea spread, slowly at first, through different movements, each in its own way. Today, in Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative synagogues, a girl may read from the Torah scroll itself, just as a boy does. In Orthodox communities that mark it, it happens in other ways: a girl gives a talk on a passage she has studied, or celebrates with women and family, or takes on a project of learning or kindness. The Torah itself imagines everyone gathered to hear it: "Assemble the people, the men and the women and the little ones, and thy stranger that is within thy gates, that they may hear, and that they may learn." A girl at a lectern on a Shabbat morning is one way of answering that verse.
screen: `DAUGHTER OF THE COMMANDMENT.` · `A PRINTED BOOK, NOT THE SCROLL.` · `EACH MOVEMENT, ITS OWN WAY.` · `MEN, WOMEN AND LITTLE ONES.` · then, large: `THAT THEY MAY HEAR, AND LEARN.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: celebrate a girl's milestone. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Bring to mind a girl or young woman you know who has just done something: started a new school, learned to ride a bike, passed a test, stood up for a friend, or had her own bat mitzvah. Hold that moment for a minute, the way a community holds a girl at the lectern. Notice what she worked for. Then decide how you'll mark it: a message, a card, a word in front of the family at dinner. Something she'll hear. The bell holds the time.
The first bat mitzvah. Judith Kaplan, on a Shabbat morning in New York, saying the blessings and reading Torah as a daughter of the commandment. Today's word.
Your line: the first bat mitzvah. Today, mark one girl's milestone out loud, in front of someone. Day one thousand forty.

howItsDone: In Reform, Reconstructionist and Conservative synagogues a bat mitzvah girl may read from the Torah scroll and lead prayers; in Orthodox communities that mark it, the milestone is marked with a talk on a text she has studied, a women's gathering or a family celebration.

notes: Claims rule: 1922, New York and 'the first' come from the index title and hook. Earlier girls' ceremonies existed in some places (e.g., in Europe), so 'the first' is debated; the voice says the bat mitzvah 'walked into Jewish life', not that nothing preceded it. Please confirm the framing.
Details: she read in Hebrew and English from a printed Chumash after the regular reading, not from the scroll. Please confirm. Her own later recollection is not quoted.
The age of a girl's majority (twelve) is intentionally not stated.
'Slowly at first' and the description of how each movement marks a bat mitzvah: please confirm it is fair, especially the Orthodox examples.
